paper_title: SearchHorizonBench: A Benchmark for Search Value in AI Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AI agents must decide when another search is worth its cost. Answer-success probabilities capture question difficulty, while this decision requires estimating the additional benefit of search. We introduce SearchHorizonBench, a benchmark for learning and evaluating search value from execution experience. Paired continuations and repeated executions separate expected search gain from generation noise and connect prediction quality to decision utility. The resource contains 45,632 executions across 3,168 questions. On 1,632 held-out questions, historical calibration reduces Brier error by 16.2%, with the improvement concentrated in success-level information. Search gains have a standard deviation of 21.4 percentage points, and tested historical estimators explain less than 2% of this variance in point estimates. Matched-configuration learning curves probe this distinction across training scales. At the reference token price, free selection observations yield a 2.49-point utility opportunity over the best constant action, driven primarily by gain information. Reusable histories, frozen splits, strong baselines and scoring tools provide a common foundation for developing and evaluating value-aware search agents.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Large-scale agentic search logs document iterative query refor-
mulation and lexical links to earlier retrieved context [25]. Each
additional search can resolve a missing relation or entity while con-
suming time and money. In Test-400, permitting search increases
reference-equivalent answer success from 69.38% to 73.56% and
mean actor tokens from 1,069 to 6,829. Search-value prediction
identifies which questions justify that additional information cost.
SearchHorizonBench defines search value as the expected reward
difference between continuing with search and answering from
the same public history. The actor completes a chosen continua-
tion; the forecaster estimates its outcome. Three measurements
describe their behavior. Action-success prediction measures cor-
rectness under each continuation. Gain prediction measures their
difference. Decision utility combines the selected reward with the
cost of acquiring its information. Calibration captures question dif-
ficulty; paired gain and cost measurements identify the information
relevant to choosing further search.
sections.content: The benchmark connects these measurements through native paired executions. Every saved state supports both continuations, 1 repeated outcomes, fixed reference answers and recorded resource costs. Historical action means and task priors establish strong references. Repeated executions separate expected-gain error from generation noise. Matched-configuration learning curves measure the effect of additional training data. decision-information factorial independently varies access to query-specific gains and queryspecific costs. These controls give search-value estimators common test of prediction accuracy and decision utility. Paired evaluation identifies which information calibration improves. On Test-1632, historical correction reduces Brier from 0.2145 to 0.1797. Task priors account for 88.9% of that change, and success-level prediction accounts for 99.9%. Search gains vary substantially across questions, with standard deviation of 21.4 percentage points. The calibrated historical predictors explain less than 2% of this variation in point estimates. The evaluated regressors remain near zero gain skill across same-actor, same-backend training sets of 20 to 1,100 questions. These results establish question-specific gain prediction as distinct benchmark target. Gain information identifies opportunities for cost-aware search. At token price of 0.005 per thousand tokens, sample-informed selector gains 2.49 utility percentage points over the best constant action. Holding cost information fixed and varying gain information retains 2.48 points; varying cost alone gives 0.68 points. deployable two-answer consistency rule pays for its probes, making signal acquisition part of evaluation. SearchHorizonBench contributes the paired-execution resource, controlled account of difficulty and gain information, and an evaluation connecting that information to decisions. Its 45,632 executions and 8,880 forecasts cover 3,168 questions across actors, retrieval backends, budgets and rewards.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Retrieval decisions and agent control. Self-RAG, FLARE, DRAGIN and Adaptive-RAG develop retrieval triggers or strategy selection [2, 15, 16, 36]. Search-R1 and R2-Searcher train search policies with reinforcement learning [17, 47]. Stop-RAG, HALT, TASR and Agentic Abstention study stopping through values, verification, stability or confidence [18, 22, 30, 34]. SearchJev scores legal search decisions [4]. SearchHorizonBench supplies aligned executions for measuring future action value and the experience needed to estimate it. Execution-derived utility. Calibration Is Not Control studies intervention value through matched-prefix execution and evaluates learned controllers [46]. CoBRA learns tool-use boundaries from paired internal and external trajectories [50]. Search-G1 trains intervention-calibrated readouts of retrieval necessity and evidence reliance [5]. Tian et al. predict answer quality and changes across observed retrieval iterations [37], and Wu et al. model tool necessity, utility, and affordability [42]. Bridge Evidence measures documents contribution to later agent actions [24]; reader-specific utility research examines how evidence preferences and intervention effects transfer [49]. Matched revision studies separate re-solving, scaffolding and draft content [28]; repeat-aware QA audits separate source-induced answer changes from within-source variation [26]. SkillLearnBench evaluates experience-derived agent skills at content, trajectory and task-outcome levels [48]. SearchHorizonBench measures prospective action-value prediction and historical reuse with repeated outcomes and matched historical baselines. Ning, Li, and Kong Budgets, configuration selection, and calibration. Budget-aware control and active-retrieval evaluation account for information costs [11, 23, 32, 43]. Evaluation-budget studies allocate questions, trajectories and repeated answers to improve precision [27]. DRAG selects retrievergenerator configurations [1]. Pandoras Router and stage-aware pruning price value estimation and context use [12, 19]. Search as Computation Allocation formalizes costly information acquisition [40]. THERMOMETER and CALIBFORMER transfer probability calibration across tasks and models [10, 35]. Our statistical tools build on treatment-effect estimation, queryperformance prediction, calibration and U-statistics [3, 6, 14, 20].

sections.title:
3 Learning from Agent Executions
3.1 A shared state and two executable actions
A state 𝑥 is the complete public interaction history available to
the agent, including tool responses and returned reasoning text.
A checkpoint is a saved state at a legal action boundary. At each
checkpoint, Think reasons with existing evidence and returns an
answer. Search may retrieve further evidence before answering.
The actor, action instructions, retrieval interface, and remaining
budget define the execution being predicted.

Their difference is the expected gain from further search. This gain includes the complete continuation, including query planning, returned evidence, and final answer generation. The main actor uses enabled reasoning, an 8,192-token completion budget, and at most three additional searches. Both branches start from the same history. Malformed forecasts use the fixed pair (0.5, 0.5). Transport errors remain incomplete until recovered. Reference answers and future retrieval results belong to the evaluation data.

sections.title:
4 Benchmark and Evaluation
4.1 Questions, histories, and transfer settings
Test-400 contains 120 development and 400 test questions, balanced
across HotpotQA bridge and comparison questions and MuSiQue
questions requiring two, three, or four reasoning hops [38, 45]. Sup-
porting Wikipedia pages are disjoint between development and test.
We save the initial state and states reached after the first and second
actual search. Test counts at these checkpoints are 400, 377, and 171.
Later checkpoints describe the population of agents that reaches
them; repeated-question comparisons preserve that dependence.
sections.content: Test-1632 contains 1,632 questions with reference-support screening before execution. It includes 400 questions in each of the first four strata and all 32 eligible four-hop questions. Each stratum receives weight 0.2. The frozen source map uses the original 120 Tavily-search questions; target execution uses DeepSeek search. separate 40/400 development/test study covers Natural Questions queries [21]. The benchmark also varies completion budgets of 8,192 or 16,384 tokens and search limits of three or six. The component study uses 128 development and 320 test questions at real pending query. Flash and Pro each execute STOP, DeepSeek search, and Serper search. STOP cancels the pending call and answers; the two search actions execute its query and then answer. Four repetitions produce 10,752 executions. shared STOP execution supports both backend comparisons. ClueWeb22 and FineWeb supply two additional indexed-source conditions on 32 development and 64 test states [7, 29, 31]. These comparisons preserve the query and limit each returned packet to five documents with at most 1,500 characters each. collection study uses 32 development and 96 test tasks from DeepSearchQA [13]. The actor must return set of requested items. We compare stopping, executing the pending query on the same source, and switching the query to another source. The reward is set F1, the harmonic mean of precision and recall against curated reference items. Four repetitions of three actions yield 1,536 outcomes. The resource contains 45,632 distinct executions and 8,880 forecasts across 3,168 distinct questions; shared executions count once. Appendix provides the inventory.

sections.title:
4.2 Scoring and comparison costs
The common evaluation target is correctness equivalent to the
frozen reference answer, scored by the fixed Flash reference-
equivalence rule. Normalized exact matches, explicit abstentions
and terminal failures receive automatic scores; the remaining dis-
tinct question–answer pairs receive semantic judgments. Identical
answers share a label. In the actor–retriever audit, two context-
isolated AI panels reviewed 812 distinct answers and achieved
agreement 95.4%, with 𝜅 = 0.918. Their source-support and
answer-equivalence assessments remain separate. A deterministic
containment check and exact match evaluate alternative lexical
targets in Appendix C.

5.3 The gain-prediction gap persists with more
sections.content: training The same-configuration experiment controls training scale and backend mismatch. It predicts held-out Test-1632 initial states using 201,100 training questions from the same Flash actor and DeepSeek search configuration. Raw-score polynomial ridge, publicfeature ridge and frozen MiniLM text ridge directly regress the observed gain. Three training-only folds choose regularization; mean guard also evaluates selecting constant predictor. Four outer component folds and ten nested samples produce separate fits at every training budget. Public-feature ridge improves from 1.67% gain 𝑅2 at 120 questions to +0.72% at 1,100, with final interval [1.78, 3.09]%. Raw-score ridge reaches +0.27%, and the guarded text model selects the mean at the largest budget. Figure 4 shows the full 5 curves. The tested families remain near the constant-gain reference across these matched-configuration training budgets. The curves establish common learning-scale reference for evaluating richer decision signals.

sections.title: 5.4 Gain information drives price-sensitive
sections.content: opportunity The decision factorial separates the information needed for pricesensitive search. Its four rules use fixed or query-specific gain estimates, crossed with fixed or query-specific token estimates. Queryspecific values use two selection draws per action; the other two draws evaluate the choice. Fixed values come from forty separate same-configuration development questions. All four rules use the same held-out reward and cost, so their comparison identifies the value of the information supplied for selection. At 𝜆 = 0.005, gain information with fixed costs gives +2.48 utility points over the best constant, with interval [1.28, 3.52]. Cost information with fixed gain gives +0.68 points, with interval [0.64, 1.73]. Both together give +2.49 points; adding cost information to gain information changes utility by +0.012 points, with interval [0.025, 0.051]. Adding gain information to cost-only selection yields +1.81 points, with interval [1.10, 2.65]. Gain information identifies low-value searches whose cost can be saved. Figure 5 keeps the five valuations visible and evaluates gain and decision skill separately. Disjoint selection and evaluation draws quantify decision opportunity with free selection observations. The selectors four labeled selection executions are excluded from acquisition cost, and its expected value is bounded above by the ideal policy with exact action values. At zero token price, always SEARCH defines the accuracy reference; the selectors difference is 0.36 points with interval [1.42, 0.55]. sections.title: 5.5 Useful decision signals must cover their
sections.content: acquisition cost Two-probe consistency selects THINK when two valid normalized THINK answers agree and SEARCH otherwise. Agreement occurs in 65.0% of probe pairs. Before charging probes, the selected continuation saves 3,451 tokens relative to always SEARCH. The probes consume 2,210, leaving 1,241 net tokens saved at 1.87point success cost. Utility is 1.25 points at 0.005, with interval [2.38, 0.35]. The benchmark evaluates signal quality together with its acquisition cost.

sections.title: 5.6 A common benchmark spans execution
sections.content: settings The broader resource tests the same quantities under different agent configurations. Indexed retrieval yields Brier 0.1417 on ClueWeb and 0.1498 on FineWeb, against historical means 0.1982 and 0.1981. Qwen actors and forecasters add separate model family. Budget interventions distinguish evidence effects from generation capacity; increasing the search limit from three to six at 8k tokens raises length failures by 2.5 points, while 16k budget removes that increase. Collection-completion tasks use bounded set F1 and three actions. Their selected mean-gain predictor and constant STOP policy provide reward-specific references. These settings extend the benchmarks success, gain and decision measurements while retaining each execution and reward definition.

sections.title:
6 Using the Benchmark
SearchHorizonBench provides public histories and action defini-
tions for new forecasters. Researchers fit their models on develop-
ment outcomes, then submit action-success probabilities or signed
gain predictions for held-out states. Evaluation uses separate out-
come records and supporting-page groups. The value scorer reports
sections.content: 6 success error and generation-noise-corrected gain error; the policy scorer charges prediction and continuation tokens. Saved baselines, fixed priors and reusable splits support direct method comparisons. Scoring success, gain and utility on matched executions makes forecasters contribution to search decisions directly testable.

sections.title:
7 Conclusion
SearchHorizonBench establishes a reusable evaluation of when
further Web search is worthwhile. Shared histories, repeated con-
tinuations and explicit costs connect success prediction, generation-
noise-corrected gain estimation and decision utility. The resource
spans 45,632 executions. On 1,632 held-out questions, historical
calibration improves Brier error by 16.2%, with task priors account-
ing for 88.9% of that change. A search-gain standard deviation
of 21.4 percentage points and less than 2% explained variance in
tested historical estimators establish a distinct prediction target.
Matched-configuration learning curves provide controlled compar-
isons across training scales. At the reference token price, factorized
decisions identify a 2.49-point free-observation opportunity driven
primarily by gain information. The benchmark’s public inputs,
frozen splits, historical controls and scoring tools make the contribu-
tion of execution experience to search decisions directly testable.

Figure 6 counts shared STOP executions once; questions reused across settings retain their identity. Public predictor records contain histories, actor identity, and action definitions. Evaluation records contain reference answers, observed rewards, support groups, and resource measurements. Saved queries and retrieval responses fix the evidence available to repeated executions. The released value scorer evaluates probability and gain predictions; the policy scorer also charges prediction tokens. Complete prediction matrices, per-case judgments, all pricing settings, and machine-readable manifests accompany the resource. AI assistance and reproduction. DeepSeek supplies executions, forecasts and grading; Qwen supplies cross-family controls. AI also assists auditing, coding, analysis and writing. Scorers and figure sources reproduce the reported comparisons. Question populations. The Test-400 strata contain 24 development and 80 test questions each. Official source splits contribute 160 HotpotQA validation questions, 212 MuSiQue development questions, and 28 MuSiQue training questions to the study test cohort. Its study-development questions and supporting pages are separate. Flash generates the source histories. Later checkpoints and other actors therefore evaluate continuations conditional on Flash reaching those states. The initial-state, first-search and second-search Test-400 populations contain 400, 377 and 171 questions. Their development populations contain 120, 114 and 40. The matched Pro subset contains 80, 74 and 32 reached test states. Source qualification uses the complete supporting paragraphs. Flash first solves question with its reference hidden; Flash and Pro then assess reference support separately. Fixed ranks select the eligible cases before actor execution. The Test-1632 campaign screens 8,000 candidates, of which 3,380 receive independent source review and 2,325 are supported. The available four-hop pool yields 32 independently supported questions; all enter the 1,632-question cohort. The five strata receive equal weight, and 1,081 supportingpage components determine resampling. An additional overlap sensitivity removes 149 questions sharing prior method-selection page and retains 1,483 questions. Its four-hop stratum has one component, so its equal-stratum analysis reports point estimates. The Natural Questions extension selects 40 development and 400 test queries after source support, standalone clarity and temporal-stability checks. Test pages form 398 components and are development-disjoint. The actorretriever study selects 128 development and 320 test questions after valid pending query is reached. Its 848 supporting pages are mutually disjoint and separate from prior labeled studies. This conditional population excludes source trajectories that already answer. The indexed extension samples 32 development and 64 test states by fixed family-stratified rank. Model and retrieval settings. The DeepSeek request identifiers are deepseek-flash and deepseek-v4-pro; records also retain served-model identifiers. Main continuations use enabled reasoning Ning, Li, and Kong and an 8,192-token total completion budget. The factorial study crosses 8,192/16,384 tokens with three/six permitted searches. Tavily uses basic search with five snippets. Component comparisons normalize DeepSeek and Serper results to five documents and 1,500 characters per document. ClueWeb uses configured shards 03 with cw22_a=false, and FineWeb uses seven shards. Stored responses, timestamps and returned crawl metadata define these indexed conditions. DeepSeek requests omit temperature, top-𝑝 and seed. The providers documented thinking mode ignores temperature. Its current top-𝑝 behavior is model-dependent; Pro thinking fixes top-𝑝 at 0.95 with tools and 1.0 otherwise, while Flash non-thinking fixes it at 1.0 [9]. Flash thinking allows top-𝑝 in [0.95, 1]. The historical responses do not echo an effective sampler configuration. We therefore distinguish logged request settings from provider behavior documented on October 25, 2026. Actor requests enable high-effort reasoning; main forecasts disable reasoning with 2,048token cap. Repetitions are distinct requests with cached evidence. Conditional generation independence is the statistical assumption; shared identical answers retain one correctness judgment. Independent model family. Qwen3-4B Q4_K_M uses the pinned revision bc640142c66e and llama.cpp b11669. Actor sampling enables reasoning with temperature 0.6, top-𝑝 0.95, top-𝑘 20, 16,384token context and 8,192-token continuation budget. Forecaster sampling disables reasoning with temperature 0.7, top-𝑝 0.8, top-𝑘 20 and 2,048-token cap. The 120 Qwen forecasts use the same public inputs as the DeepSeek forecasters. The actor extension fixes 240 DeepSeek forecasts and 3,360 fitted probability pairs before Qwen test execution. Its 640 test outputs contain 610 valid answers, nine length failures and 21 malformed outputs; these failure statuses receive zero reward.

sections.content: Calibration and input controls. All fits use development labels. Shared-input maps use both raw probabilities; independent affine maps use one per action. shared-input control selects separate penalty for each action. Logistic, beta and isotonic controls provide standard calibration alternatives [20]. Direct-gain models regress the action difference; residual models adjust historical map. The release specifies the inputs and fitting grid for each model. Historical and public-input controls. Stratum means use 24 development questions per category. Metadata ridge uses dataset family, comparison membership and hop count. Public-prefix features include both probabilities, log question and tool-text lengths, lexical evidence gap and query/document novelty. The gap is the fraction of question terms absent from tool text. Query novelty is one minus Jaccard overlap with previous queries; document novelty is the fraction of new identifiers. Both are zero before two searches. Four development folds select regularization from {0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100}; all controls use the original 120 development questions. Levels and gains. The learned-level control predicts the average success probability and assigns historical mean gain. In the component study, clipping the two reconstructed probabilities to [0, 1] can also change their level and intended gain. This occurs on 31 of 320 questions for the reverse Flash mean-gain control. The exact 8 SearchHorizonBench Figure 6: Execution coverage and the source/target setting. Each scoring rule defines its own reward and gain population. Dependence and uncertainty. Equations 4 and 5 use independent generation draws conditional on the cached evidence. Repeated identical answers retain shared judgment. Supporting-page components define the bootstrap units. Each resample retains all linked questions, actions, checkpoints and repeated labels. Fixed-predictor intervals describe evaluation variation conditional on fitted parameters. The supervision-budget study additionally reports variation over twenty training subsets; its intervals condition on those fits. Analysis provenance. The released records retain original comparison definitions, source timestamps, fixed historical predictions and later cross-validation splits. Frozen MiniLM sentence embeddings [33, 41] use question text at the initial checkpoint and include the available assistant/tool history at later checkpoints. Ridge and 200-tree forest heads estimate action probabilities or their difference. Confidence, entropy, query/document novelty and evidencegap signals use public observations with development-selected thresholds. Evaluator-stratum means use the task category as an explanatory control. Initial-checkpoint Brier is 0.1899 for those means, 0.2035 for the global mean and 0.1836 for the shared-input map.
